[MUJAHID:v1p326#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | The idolater calls to water with his tongue and gestures toward it with his hands, but it never comes to him.
[MUQATIL:13:14/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The true invocation means the declaration of sincerity and divine unity.
[MUQATIL:13:14/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Those invoked besides God are the idols that people worship.
[MUQATIL:13:14/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Idols neither answer their worshippers nor benefit them, like water that a thirsty man at a well's edge calls toward his mouth but cannot reach, until he dies of thirst.
[MUQATIL:13:14/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Calling the idols means worshipping them, and the worship of disbelievers is loss and falsehood.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a redundant preposition or لا, the exception follows the governed noun's syntactic case, as its substitute, rather than the preposition's surface case; the alternative wording with من is unavailable.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ما أنت بشيء إلا شيء, Tamim has شيء in the nominative slot while Hijaz has it accusative; when the dialects coincide, Sibawayh favors the underlying syntactic case.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With لست بشيء إلا شيئا, the exception is accusative as though باء were absent; the cited line demonstrates باء before an accusative predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In لا أحد فيها إلا عبد الله, the exception substitutes for the nominative مبتدأ slot; the construction answers هل من أحد, and a definite name cannot be directly coordinated with لا.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In لا أحد رأيته إلا زيد, whether رأيته is the predicate or an adjective, the analysis makes the initial noun equivalent to لا أحد مرئي or لا أحد مرئيا.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hijazi ما and إن cannot be reordered like verbs because they are particles; a long construction can nevertheless make otherwise difficult word order acceptable.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أحد is normally confined to negation, so إن أحدا لا يقول ذاك is weak because negation follows an affirmative opening; it is tolerated when the whole sense is negative.
[SIBAWAYH:لاعلىماعملفيالاسمولكنالاسموماعملفيهفيموضعاسممرفوعأو#375/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After إن أحدا لا يقول, إلا زيدا can substitute for the initial noun under the negative sense, or إلا زيد can attach to يقول; the latter is weaker than constructions that begin with negation.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلهعلىألفدرهمعرفاms158|ومثلذلكقولالأحوص#177/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In دعوة الحق, the annexed verbal noun reiterates that the preceding expression الله أكبر is a true invocation.
[FARRA:v2p60/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | دعوة الحق means the testimony لا إله إلا الله.
[FARRA:v2p60/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The idols cannot answer their callers, like a thirsty person reaching toward water without a way to draw it; the water still cannot reach his mouth.
[MAJAZ:v1p325/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | This means those who call on someone other than God. Dūnahu is used like ʿanhu, “away from Him,” as the cited poet’s dūnī means ʿannī.
[MAJAZ:v1p325/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Lā yastajībūn means they do not answer; Kaʿb’s verse uses istajābah in this sense.
[MAJAZ:v1p327/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The comparison is to someone reaching for water with open hands, who cannot deliver it to his mouth or gather it with his fingers. The cited poets use the futile water-grasping image for something unobtainable.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda explains “the true call” as the testimony that there is no god but God.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334/r2] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās also glosses “the true call” as “there is no god but God.”
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334/r3] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the outstretched hands cannot bring water to the mouth while they remain extended and do not close around it.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p334/r4] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says this is a parable for taking a god besides God: it will neither benefit nor protect its worshipper, who dies persisting in that practice.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p226#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The idolaters get nothing from the beings they call, just as water cannot be retained in a hand to carry it to the mouth.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p226#2/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Arabs use grasping water as an idiom for seeking what cannot be obtained; the cited anonymous poem gives the same image.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p226#2/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | In the poem, lam tasqihi means it did not carry the water; wasq means carrying or loading.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p141/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The supplicant is like someone stretching hands toward water to scoop it and bring it to his mouth; that action is left implicit.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p141/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · ضابئ | reports | Ḍābiʾ’s poem compares longing without fulfillment to clutching water that the fingers cannot hold; Arabs use the same expression for futile pursuit.
[TAB-FULL:v13p485/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The true call belongs to Allah; al-Tabari identifies it as affirming God's oneness and testifying that there is no deity but Allah.
[TAB-FULL:v13p485/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The phrase means the call itself is the truth, expressed through an iḍāfa like دار الآخرة in 12:109. | mentions 12:109
[TAB-FULL:v13p485/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas interprets the true call as لا إله إلا الله, or the testimony that there is no deity but Allah.
[TAB-FULL:v13p485/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · علي | reports | Ali interprets the true call as monotheism.

[TAB-FULL:v13p485/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says only Allah merits the true call and that none should be called a deity besides Him.
[TAB-FULL:v13p487#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The invoked idols do not answer requests for benefit or protection from harm; calling on them is as useless as extending empty hands to water without drawing it into a vessel.
[TAB-FULL:v13p487#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The image evokes an impossible effort; Arabs liken pursuing what cannot be attained to grasping water, as the cited poems illustrate.
[TAB-FULL:v13p487#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · علي | reports | Ali compares the image to a thirsty man reaching into a well and hoping the water will rise to him, which it cannot do.
[TAB-FULL:v13p487#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the person calls to the water with his tongue and gestures with his hand, but it never comes; so too those invoked besides Allah do not answer.
[TAB-FULL:v13p487/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Those called upon besides Allah are idols that polytheists invoke as lords and gods; min dunihi means apart from Allah, and these deficient objects cannot be gods, since only Allah is God. The cited usage of dun means falling short of someone. | mentions 4:117
[TAB-FULL:v13p489#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Calling on an idol or stone never brings good or wards off harm, and the worshipper remains without benefit until death, like one who dies thirsty with outstretched arms.
[TAB-FULL:v13p489#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | One report from Ibn Abbas compares the polytheist to a thirsty man who sees his reflection in distant water and cannot grasp it.
[TAB-FULL:v13p489#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Another report from Ibn Abbas pictures a dying thirsty person's hands in water but unable to reach his mouth; likewise idols never answer or benefit their worshippers.
[TAB-FULL:v13p489#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says the idols do no more good than hands extended toward something that can never be reached.
[TAB-FULL:v13p489#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says water cannot reach the mouth while the hands remain outstretched, just as an adopted deity cannot benefit its worshipper or protect him from harm until death.
[TAB-FULL:v13p489/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada depicts the water as unreachable until the thirsty person tears his neck apart and dies of thirst.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p143/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · التفسير | reports | A reported explanation identifies the true invocation as the testimony that there is no god but God.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p143/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Zajjāj also allows that the true invocation is a monotheist's prayer to God, which God answers.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p143/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Idols answer no prayers; calling them is like a thirsty person asking water to reach his mouth, though water cannot respond or arrive.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p143/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعضهم | reports | Another account pictures a person at a well's edge calling water from its bottom to his mouth; Zajjāj says the two explanations amount to the same thing.
[NAHHAS:v2p353/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Daʿwā al-kāfirīn means their calling upon idols, which is futile, far from right and unable to bring a response.
[RUMMANI:v1p82/r4] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | The image joins need for a benefit

[BAQILLANI:v1p123/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Literary experts can identify who follows another in diction, meaning, or both, and who adopts another’s style or merely resembles it.
[BAQILLANI:v1p123/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Examples include al-Buḥturī’s borrowing from Abū Tammām, Abū Tammām’s borrowing from Abū Nuwās and Muslim, and poets who freely borrow from many sources.
[BAQILLANI:v1p123/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Al-Mutanabbī’s denial of borrowing cannot fool experts, who point out every word or allusion he took from the Ṭāʾiyyayn.
[BAQILLANI:v1p123/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Experts distinguish direct borrowing from resemblance of style, describing degrees of similarity from near-identical to as far apart as east and west.
[BAQILLANI:v1p123/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Because experts know literary genres and their limits in fine detail, they cannot miss speech that departs from every familiar form; confusion reflects deficient expertise.
[BAQILLANI:v1p123/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | A modern claimant’s boast of surpassing al-Buḥturī, Abū Nuwās, or Muslim does not establish mastery; these poets differ greatly, and conceit does not diminish al-Buḥturī.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | The sermon compares the inviolability of Muslims’ blood, property, and honor to the sacred day, month, and place, lasting until the final meeting.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r10] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | He asks whether he has conveyed the message, instructs witnesses to inform absentees, and notes a later recipient may understand better than the hearer.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | He forbids mutual wrongdoing and says a Muslim’s property is lawful only with its owner’s willing consent.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | All pre-Islamic blood claims are annulled, beginning with the blood claim for Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith, killed by Hudhayl while nursed among Banū Layth.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | All pre-Islamic usury is annulled, beginning with the debt of his uncle al-ʿAbbās; creditors may claim principal without wronging or being wronged. | mentions 2:279
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | The calendar has returned to its original arrangement; the sermon cites the four sacred months and warns against wronging oneself in them. | mentions 9:36
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | He warns Muslims not to revert to killing one another as unbelievers; Satan has despaired of being worshipped by the praying but still seeks to stir conflict.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r7] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | The sermon describes wives as entrusted dependents, sets reciprocal rights, forbids admitting unwanted guests to the marital bed, and prescribes admonition, bed separation, and non-injurious striking for feared nushūz. | mentions 4:34
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | Husbands owe wives customary provision and clothing; the marriage bond was taken under God’s trust and made lawful by God’s word.
[BAQILLANI:v1p130#2/r9] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · النبي | reports | A person holding a trust must return it to its owner.
[SULAMI:v1p329#4/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | The most truthful calls are God's calls: answering the call of truth brings one to God, while answering the ego's calls leads to ruin.
[SULAMI:v1p329#4/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | The caller of truth guides without Satan's or the ego's share; when its call is fulfilled, lights of truth leave the one called without doubt.
[SULAMI:v1p329#4/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The caller of truth calls by means of the Real and toward the Real.
[SULAMI:v1p329#4/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر | reports | Calls that summon through truth, toward truth, or to its path direct people to truth; whoever calls by himself calls only to himself and is astray.

[THALABI:v5p280/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Daʿwat al-ḥaqq means the true invocation; the phrase joins two different nouns.

[QUSHAYRI:v2p102/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | In the spiritual path, the soul’s promptings call to a kind of idolatry: seeing something of oneself, imagining claims for oneself, dwelling in separation, and being blind to the realities of union.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p323/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عبيد وابن قتيبة | reports | Abu Ubayd and Ibn Qutayba explain the image as an Arabic proverb for striving after something unattainable: water cannot be retained in a grasping hand.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p323/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عبيد وابن قتيبة | reports | On this proverb reading, the idolaters gain nothing from their invocation, just as a person grasping water holds nothing.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p324/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عبيدة وابن الأنباري | reports | Abu Ubayda glosses the poem’s verb as “to confront”; Ibn al-Anbari explains the phrase as collecting, carrying, or conveying the water.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p324/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The cited Arabic line compares yearning for the absent beloved to trying to draw water with one’s fingertips, illustrating the futile grasping-water proverb.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p324/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A second poem likewise likens lost affection to someone holding water in the hand, supporting the proverb’s sense.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p324/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba says the verse is elliptical: it means stretching one’s palms toward water to grasp it, or grasping it to bring it to one’s mouth.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:13:13-14/r10] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Their invocation is as futile as someone beckoning water to reach his mouth: the water cannot reach it by being called.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:13:13-14/r11] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The disbelievers' worship of idols ends in ruin and is futile.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:13:13-14/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God alone is rightly invoked by His creation; the true invocation is the declaration that there is no god but God.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:13:13-14/r9] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Those who invoke besides God are the polytheists calling on idols.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p311/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The Shammakh's line praises generosity: its raised banner is the glory sought by ʿAraba, who supplied the poet with provisions, rather than a military contest.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p311/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | rejects | Reading the right hand as sheer physical strength would suit a context of force and battle better than this praise of generosity.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p311/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The right hand can signal deliberate care and seriousness because it is the honored, stronger hand and the one people begin with when pursuing an aim.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p311/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Buhturi's line about his hand being in the patron's right hand supports this image of entrusted agency; Jurjani identifies the patron as Yunus ibn Bugha, favored by al-Muʿtazz.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p311/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | reports | Jurjani adds Sulayman ibn Qutta's address to Banu Taym as a further contextual test in the discussion of right-hand imagery and intended action.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p293/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Eloquence cannot arise from bare word order: joining ضحك and خرج would add nothing unless their grammatical meanings and relations create a particular construction.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p293/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The claim that meanings do not increase while words do is coherent only if verbal increase means the qualities produced by observing grammatical meanings; bare sounds cannot increase in merit.
[DAMGHANI:v1p69/r3] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | The image of stretching one's hands to water means reaching from a distance.
[JISHUMI:v5p3766/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The genitive construction دعوة الحق is used although الدعوة itself is الحق, because the two nouns differ, like مسجد الجامع and the cited phrase ولدار الآخرة. | mentions 12:109
[JISHUMI:v5p3766/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Istijaba and ijaba both mean answering, but istijaba also carries the sense of seeking or requesting.
[JISHUMI:v5p3766/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشاعر | reports | The poet's use of يستجبه witnesses the sense of responding to a call for help.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس، وقتادة، وابن زيد | reports | Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd identify دعوة الحق as the testimony of divine oneness, there is no god but Allah.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو علي | reports | Abu Ali understands the image as someone trying to reach water with an outstretched hand.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the person dies before he can reach the water.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · علي، وعطاء، وأبو مسلم | reports | Ali, Ata, and Abu Muslim picture a thirsty person at a well without a bucket, reaching for water that neither comes up nor reaches him; likewise idols neither answer nor benefit their worshippers.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas compares them to a thirsty person who sees water far away but cannot reach it.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · القاضي | prefers | The judge's closest reading is someone gesturing toward water and hoping it will reach his mouth, though it cannot.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس | reports | Al-Dahhak, reporting from Ibn Abbas, says an outstretched hand cannot help a thirsty person, just as idols can neither benefit nor harm their worshippers.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r16] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو عبيدة، والقتبي، وأبو مسلم، وأبو القاسم | reports | They explain the image as a person pursuing what cannot be attained, like someone grasping water; a poem uses the same comparison for lost affection.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r17] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الشاعر | reports | The poet compares former affection to someone clutching water in his hand, illustrating an unattainable thing.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The phrase in ضلال has been explained as being in ruin or perdition.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r19] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another explanation is that the unbelievers' invocation strays from what is correct.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan explains that Allah is the Real, so whoever calls on Him has called on truth.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | A further gloss is that it misses the path to answer and benefit, and thus departs from the true invocation.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another explanation says that whoever calls on God calls on a living, powerful, hearing, knowing, seeing being, so the invocation is true and not lost.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another gloss is that God's worship is the truth because no other being deserves worship.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Another interpretation is an invocation made with a sound expectation of an answer, and such a prayer is heard and answered.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | A further gloss is th

[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Those who call on others besides God are the polytheists who have made idols into lords.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says they call on idols to meet their needs.
[JISHUMI:v5p3767/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد، والأصم | reports | Mujahid and al-Asamm compare idol worshippers to someone calling to water and gesturing with his hand, but the water does not come.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The true, sincere invocation belongs to God.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says hands spread in water do not help a thirsty person unless he scoops it; this depicts the disbelievers' frustration.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · علي | reports | Ali explains the true invocation as monotheism.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas identifies the true invocation as the testimony that there is no god but God.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is sincere supplication, which can be directed only to God.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Those invoked besides God are idols worshipped instead of Him.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The idols answer no request for benefit or for warding off harm.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Cupped hands cannot hold water or bring it to the mouth; idol worshippers likewise gain nothing from powerless idols.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid likens the worshipper to a thirsty person who sees distant water, gestures and calls, but never reaches it.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p305#2/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · علي وعطاء | reports | Ali and Ata compare the idolater to a thirsty person at a well who cannot reach its water, and whose call cannot make water rise.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p306/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The disbelievers' invocation is directed to their idols, which abandon them when needed; the verse echoes the statement that their fabrications disappear. | mentions 6:24
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p306/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس | reports | Al-Dahhak reports Ibn Abbas explaining this as disbelievers' prayer to their Lord being lost because their voices are screened from God.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | One reading attaches the call to truth, like كلمة الحق: it is exclusively true, and God answers and grants what benefits the petitioner because He alone is worthy of prayer.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r10] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A variant reads تدعون with direct address instead of the third-person form.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r11] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Another reported reading places nunation on باسط.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r12] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | ضلال is loss without benefit: unbelievers' calls to God receive no answer, while their idols cannot answer them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Alternatively, it is the call directed to the True One, God, who hears and answers.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says al-Haqq means God, and every invocation directed to Him is the true invocation.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The phrase connects with the account of Arbad: the thunderbolt was God's unseen counterplot, and the Prophet's prayer against the two men was answered. | mentions 13:13
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet prayed that God strike Arbad and his companion as He wished; the prayer was answered, making it a true invocation.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | On the first interpretation, the verse threatens unbelievers with God's destruction and with His answering the Prophet if he prays against them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Those invoked besides God are the idols worshipped by unbelievers.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Their helplessness resembles a person extending both hands to water and asking it to reach his mouth: water cannot sense or answer thirst, and neither can idols.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p490/r9] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | Alternatively, the image is of someone spreading his fingers into water to scoop a drink, yet gathering none and failing to satisfy his request.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The pronoun ‘to Him’ refers to God.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The unbelievers’ invocation ends in loss and misguidance and brings no benefit.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains the true call as ‘There is no god but God’; Ibn Atiyya extends this to any part of religious law with the same meaning.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali ibn Abi Talib says the true call is monotheism.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The phrase may also mean that God alone receives the servants’ true invocation, whereas invocation of idols is false.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | ‘Those whom they call’ refers to objects worshipped apart from God; ‘they call’ refers to Quraysh and other Arabs.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · اليزيدي عن أبي عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Al-Yazidi reports that Abu Amr read ‘you call’ with a second-person tāʾ; yastajibūn means ‘they answer,’ as supported by poetry.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Idols do not answer anything unbelievers ask for their needs and benefits; the cited poet uses the verb for answering a call.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Futile invocation is like a person beckoning water toward his mouth: it never reaches him, just as idols cannot answer or benefit their callers.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p305/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | ‘It’ may be water and ‘reaching it’ the mouth, or ‘it’ may be the mouth and the pronoun water, since the mouth cannot reach water in that posture.
[TABRISI:13:12-15/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Istijāba and ijāba both mean responding, but istijāba also conveys the act of requesting.
[TABRISI:13:12-15/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The cited line, ‘no respondent answered him then,’ illustrates istijāba as response.
[TABRISI:13:12-15/r25] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | If kāf is a particle, it modifies an implied verbal noun: an answering like the answering of someone stretching his hands to water.
[TABRISI:13:12-15/r26] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | If kāf is a noun, the estimate is ‘an answer like the answer of one who stretches his hands,’ with no pronoun in kāf.
[TABRISI:13:12-15/r27] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The lām in li-yablugha is attached to bāsiṭ kafayhi.
[TABRISI:13:12-15/r28] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The clause may mean the water does not reach his mouth, his mouth does not reach the water, or the person with outstretched hands does not obtain the water.
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس وقتادة وابن زيد | reports | One explanation identifies the true invocation as the declaration of divine unity, ‘There is no god but God.’
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reasons that God is the Real, so calling on Him is the true invocation and whoever calls Him calls the Real.
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · الجبائي | reports | Al-Jubbāʾī takes it as the invocation by which God is called upon in exclusive monotheism; God answers the sincere caller.
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Those invoked beside God are the idols and other beings whom polytheists call on to meet their needs.
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | The image compares idol worshippers hoping for benefit to someone reaching toward distant water that cannot reach his mouth; idols bring no benefit and answer no prayer.
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid pictures someone calling to water with his tongue and gesturing with his hand, but the water does not come.
[TABRISI:13:13-14/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan pictures someone reaching for water who dies before it can reach his mouth.
[TABRISI:13:14-15/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبيدة والبلخي وأبو مسلم | reports | The Arabs use ‘like one grasping water’ for striving after something unattainable.
[TABRISI:13:14-15/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · الشاعر | reports | An anonymous poet compares lost affection to someone holding water in his hand.
[TABRISI:13:14-15/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · الشاعر الآخر | reports | A second anonymous poem compares longing to water that the fingers cannot retain.
[TABRISI:13:14-15/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The unbelievers' invocation of idols leads away from truth and right guidance.
[TABRISI:13:14-15/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | Another gloss says their invocation strays from the path of response and benefit.
